Robots.txt

You might say

Limit crawler access to duplicate filter paths, but do not use robots.txt as permission for the admin area.

A root-level file that tells automated crawlers which paths they may crawl·Shopping carts and duplicate filter URLs can waste crawler requests, so robots.txt can describe crawling rules at the site root. It is guidance for crawlers that follow the rules, not a block on normal visitors, authentication, or protection for sensitive data.
Know first
URLAuthorizationSEO
Robots Exclusion Protocol
How one rule affects crawlers without becoming a site lock
robots.txt
1User-agent: *
2Disallow: /cart
3Disallow: /admin
CrawlerAllowed to crawl/products
User browserCan still request it200 OK

Disallow is not access control; private pages still need authentication and authorization.

How robots.txt is used

The file location sets its scope: robots.txt normally lives at the site root, such as https://example.com/robots.txt. Rules apply to the matching protocol, host, and port.

A crawler reads the rules before requesting: A compliant crawler uses User-agent, Allow, and Disallow to decide whether to request a path. A normal browser does not lose access because of this file.

What it is not

Robots.txt is a crawling instruction, not permission control, and it is not the same as noindex in search results. Protect admin pages, orders, and customer data with authentication, authorization, and server-side checks rather than links hidden from navigation or Disallow alone.

You can say this to an AI Agent

“

Create robots.txt at the site root to limit crawling of duplicate filter paths while keeping normal product pages crawlable. Check the file location, rule matches, and that a normal browser can still access the path. Protect admin pages and customer data with authentication and authorization, not Disallow.
